newsitem.title: EGYPT: ING Barings specialist expects correction in Cairo.
newsitem.headline: ING Barings specialist expects correction in Cairo.

text.p: The ING Barings specialist on the Egyptian market said on Wednesday he expected a big correction soon in share prices and would advise investors to take profits on some of their Egyptian stock now.

Angus Blair told a conference that the recent price rises made Egypt one of the most expensive emerging markets in the world and only strong growth in corporate earnings this spring could prevent what he called "a mild crisis of confidence".
But he ruled out the possibility of a major sell-off or a financial crisis of the kind Mexico went through in 1994.

Prices on the Egyptian stock market have been rising sharply for about six months and Blair, head of the Middle East and North Africa at ING Barings, said that P/E ratios for the most liquid stocks had risen to above 18.

"I think that over the next few months, when we receive the year-end 1996 results and the half-year results, if companies do not provide the level of earnings growth which is sufficient for a market to be at 18 times 1997 earnings then you will see a mild crisis of confidence," he said.
"You could see an outflow of investment unless companies are providing earnings growth of over 15 percent at least.
"But I don't expect to see a major sell-off of capital. I do expect to see a correction, however, not a major market fall but a big correction, and happening pretty shortly," he added.

"We would still tell our investors to remain in the market in specific stocks and take profits in others. We're not saying sell the market but the onus is going to be on companies to increase shareholder value, to increase profits," he said.
But he added: "This is not a Mexico, the economic conditions of Egypt are far too good, and far too fundamentally good for there to be a crisis of confidence."

One factors likely to support the market is Egypt's inclusion in the IFC Investable Index and the Barings Emerging Markets Index, which would make emerging market funds continue to commit a percentage of their funds to Egypt, he said.
Other investors are willing to pay "over the odds" to get into the Egyptian market for the long term, he added.
A 22-day bull run on the Egyptian market ended this week and the all-share index fell 2.2 percent on Wednesday.

On the management of the stock market, Blair said the authorities had made much progress but there was still room for improvement, especially on disclosure of company information and delays in settling transactions.

He criticised the stock exchange's practice of arbitrarily restricting share price movements to five or 10 percent a day -- a practice the authorities say they use when they do not believe that the price change is "justified".

"It is of some concern," he said. "This does cause market confusion and harms investor sentiment and the market views price capping as a market interference. There will have a much clearer indication as to why there is a limit."
He also predicted that some of more than 100 brokerage firms in Egypt would soon disappear.

"One shouldn't be surprised about this or too concerned, given that in the legislation client capital is segregated from the capital of the companies. It's important to differentiate between them in the case of the failure of a company," he said.
Blair said that when the government comes round to selling more shares in partially privatised firms, he would advise it not to try to sell the shares at the market price.

"Our advice would be sell at a discount and probably at a significant discount, if the company is to be successfully privatised. Whether it is going to be politically acceptable to do so remains to be seen," he said.
